impact: Kids get more time for family, sleep, and play.

candidates.text: Without homework, evenings are freed for rest and family.
candidates.explanation: Directly connects banning homework to the extra family time.

candidates.text: Research links heavy homework loads to student stress and lost sleep.
candidates.explanation: Evidence that removing homework supports sleep and wellbeing.

candidates.text: A Harvard study found homework raises standardized-test scores.
candidates.explanation: Impressive and real, but it argues FOR homework — it does not bridge to this impact.

candidates.text: Homework teaches time-management skills.
candidates.explanation: A point about a different impact; it does not connect to family/sleep/play time.

claim: This House would ban phones in classrooms.
impact: Students focus better and learn more.

candidates.text: Without phones, students aren't pulled away by notifications mid-lesson.
candidates.explanation: Links the ban to sustained attention, which supports learning.

candidates.text: Schools that restricted phones reported higher test results the next year.
candidates.explanation: Evidence tying the ban to improved learning outcomes.

candidates.text: Smartphones are the best-selling consumer electronic of all time.
candidates.explanation: A strong-sounding fact that has nothing to do with classroom focus.

candidates.text: Phones can be used as calculators.
candidates.explanation: Argues the other way and doesn't connect to the focus impact.

claim: This House would lower the voting age to 16.
impact: Young people become lifelong, engaged voters.

candidates.text: Voting while still in school builds a habit that carries into adulthood.
candidates.explanation: Connects early voting to lifelong engagement.

candidates.text: Turnout studies show first voting at 16-17 predicts higher lifelong turnout.
candidates.explanation: Evidence directly supporting the lifelong-engagement impact.

candidates.text: A famous economist won a Nobel Prize for work on voting systems.
candidates.explanation: Authoritative but irrelevant to whether 16-year-olds become engaged voters.

candidates.text: 16-year-olds can already drive in some places.
candidates.explanation: An analogy about maturity, not a bridge to lifelong voting engagement.

claim: This House would require school uniforms.
impact: Students focus on learning instead of fashion competition.

candidates.text: When students wear the same uniform, they stop comparing clothes and judging each other's style, freeing mental energy for classwork.
candidates.explanation: Directly links uniforms to reduced fashion distraction and increased focus on learning.

candidates.text: Schools in the UK that adopted uniforms reported a 5-10% increase in grades within a year.
candidates.explanation: Evidence showing uniforms improve academic outcomes by reducing social comparison.

candidates.text: Uniforms are worn by military personnel, flight crews, and elite athletes, demonstrating their power to build discipline and professionalism.
candidates.explanation: Sounds authoritative but does not establish a link between uniforms and classroom focus or reduced fashion pressure.

candidates.text: Uniforms are expensive to buy and sometimes hard for families to afford.
candidates.explanation: Raises a cost concern, not a bridge to the learning-focus impact.

claim: This House would increase school recess time.
impact: Students perform better academically and have improved mental health.

candidates.text: Time outdoors helps kids burn physical energy and return to class refreshed, allowing them to focus better on lessons.
candidates.explanation: Connects increased recess to classroom focus and learning readiness.

candidates.text: Research shows students who get 30+ minutes of daily unstructured play improve reading and math scores by an average of 10%.
candidates.explanation: Evidence linking play time to improved academic performance.

candidates.text: Playing sports and outdoor games teaches teamwork, leadership, and resilience—all essential life skills.
candidates.explanation: True and impressive, but these soft-skills benefits do not necessarily translate to better academic performance or mental health.

candidates.text: More recess time means fewer hours for teaching core subjects like math and reading.
candidates.explanation: Argues the opposite position and does not address the learning or mental-health impact.

claim: This House would restrict student screen time during school hours.
impact: Students concentrate better in class and retain information more effectively.

candidates.text: Without personal devices available during lessons, students' attention spans recover and they can follow along with classroom instruction for longer stretches.
candidates.explanation: Directly connects screen restrictions to improved focus and sustained attention in class.

candidates.text: Schools that banned personal devices during lessons saw test scores rise by 8% within six months, especially in reading comprehension and retention.
candidates.explanation: Evidence showing screen restrictions lead to better academic retention and test performance.

candidates.text: Technology and digital literacy are essential to modern careers and students must be prepared for a digital-first future.
candidates.explanation: Important-sounding but argues FOR unrestricted screen use during school, directly opposing the motion.

candidates.text: Screen-based learning tools help students with visual or auditory disabilities access classroom content.
candidates.explanation: Raises accessibility benefits, not a bridge to the concentration or retention impact.
